meta.subject: GERMAN
meta.author: bank-team-german
meta.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.topic: Konjunktiv I in reported speech
questions.learningObjective: Identify Konjunktiv I in reported speech
questions.stem: In the chef's recipe costing sheet, the line reads that the sauce reduces by half, so which verb form reports it indirectly?

options.text: The sauce reduces by half, says the cook.
The sauce reduce by half, the sheet notes.
The sauce reduce by half, the sheet claims.
The sauce reduced by half, the sheet states.

questions.explanation: Reported speech in German uses Konjunktiv I for the third person, so the form reduces to reduce. The indicative reduced would state a fact, while the Konjunktiv signals distance.
questions.hint: Look for the Konjunktiv I third-person ending.

questions.topic: Konjunktiv I form building
questions.stem: Write the Konjunktiv I third-person singular of kochen as it appears on the costing sheet.

answer.exemplar: The Konjunktiv I third-person singular of kochen is koche, formed from the stem koch plus the ending e, and it reports a claim without asserting it as fact.

questions.explanation: Konjunktiv I third person singular takes the stem plus e, giving koche. It marks reported information rather than a verified fact in the recipe notes.
questions.hint: Take the stem and add the Konjunktiv I ending.

questions.topic: Konjunktiv II for unreal conditions
questions.learningObjective: Recognise Konjunktiv II in unreal conditions

stimulus.body: The costing sheet notes that if the truffle weighed two kilos, the dish price would double. The chef reads this aloud.

questions.stem: Which clause carries the unreal condition in the sheet's note?

options.text: The clause about the dish price doubling.
The clause introduced by if the truffle weighed two kilos.
The clause naming the chef reading aloud.
options.misconception: confuses the reporting verb with the condition

options.text: The clause about two kilos as a fact.

questions.explanation: An unreal condition uses Konjunktiv II in the if-clause, here weighed. The result clause states the consequence, so it is not the condition itself.
questions.hint: The condition is the if-clause with Konjunktiv II.

questions.topic: Konjunktiv II for polite requests
questions.learningObjective: Use Konjunktiv II for polite requests
questions.stem: On the costing sheet, the buyer asks the supplier for a lower price, so which form is polite?

options.text: Give me a lower price now.
You give me a lower price.
options.misconception: states a fact instead of a request

options.text: Could you give me a lower price?
Might you give me a lower price?

questions.explanation: Polite requests in German use Konjunktiv II, often with modal verbs like might or could. A direct imperative or indicative statement lacks that softening distance.
questions.hint: Polite requests lean on Konjunktiv II modals.

questions.topic: Konjunktiv II in a wish
questions.learningObjective: Recognise Konjunktiv II in a wish
questions.stem: The sheet wishes the truffle cost less, so which wording expresses that wish?

options.text: The truffle costs less in reality.
If only the truffle cost less.
The truffle will cost less soon.

questions.explanation: A wish about an unreal present uses Konjunktiv II, often with if only or would that. The other tenses describe reality or time, not the wish.
questions.hint: A wish about now uses Konjunktiv II.

questions.topic: A verb of feeling with the Konjunktiv II
questions.learningObjective: Pair a feeling verb with Konjunktiv II
questions.stem: Explain how a feeling verb combines with Konjunktiv II on the costing sheet.

answer.exemplar: A verb of feeling such as wish or regret takes Konjunktiv II in the subordinate clause, because the content is unreal, and the main clause keeps the indicative, as on the chef's sheet.

questions.explanation: Feeling verbs introduce an unreal wish or regret, so the subordinate clause needs Konjunktiv II. Keeping the main clause indicative avoids double marking.
questions.hint: The feeling verb stays indicative; the wish goes Konjunktiv II.

questions.topic: The w眉rde form and its limits

stimulus.body: The sheet lists a hypothetical: would the chef sign, the price would drop. The verb sign has a simple Konjunktiv II form.

questions.stem: Why does the sheet avoid w眉rde for the verb sign?

options.text: Because w眉rde is never used in questions.
Because the verb has a simple Konjunktiv II form.
Because w眉rde only works with modals.

questions.explanation: When a verb has its own simple Konjunktiv II form, German prefers it over w眉rde. W眉rde is mainly for verbs lacking a simple form.
questions.hint: Prefer the simple form when it exists.

questions.topic: Konjunktiv I without a distinct form
questions.learningObjective: Handle verbs with no distinct Konjunktiv I
questions.stem: A verb on the sheet has no distinct Konjunktiv I, so what replaces it?
questions.explanation: When Konjunktiv I looks identical to the indicative, Konjunktiv II substitutes to keep the reported meaning clear. This avoids ambiguity in the notes.
questions.hint: Konjunktiv II substitutes for an ambiguous form.

questions.topic: A relative clause with a preposition
questions.learningObjective: Place a preposition in a relative clause
questions.stem: The sheet describes a pan the chef cooks with, so how is the preposition placed?

options.text: The pan with which the chef cooks.
The pan which the chef cooks with.
The pan that cooks with the chef.
The pan whom the chef cooks with.

questions.explanation: In German relative clauses the preposition precedes the relative pronoun, giving mit dem or mit der. Stranding the preposition is not standard German word order.
questions.hint: Preposition comes before the relative pronoun.

questions.topic: A relative pronoun in the dative
questions.stem: Choose the dative relative pronoun for a feminine noun on the sheet.

answer.exemplar: For a feminine noun in the dative, the relative pronoun is der, as in the sauce der the chef adds salt to, and it agrees in gender and number with its antecedent.

questions.explanation: Dative relative pronouns are dem, der, den, denen. For a feminine singular antecedent the form is der, which often causes confusion with the masculine nominative.
questions.hint: Feminine dative relative pronoun is der.

questions.topic: A demonstrative pronoun in a subordinate clause
questions.learningObjective: Use a demonstrative pronoun in a subordinate clause

stimulus.body: The costing sheet says the truffle is fresh, and the buyer repeats that claim in a that-clause.

questions.stem: Which demonstrative pronoun can open the reported clause?
questions.explanation: The demonstrative pronoun der can introduce a subordinate clause referring back to a statement. Dieser is a determiner here, and welcher is interrogative.
questions.hint: The pronoun der refers back to the statement.

questions.topic: A demonstrative determiner used as a pronoun
questions.stem: On the sheet, dieser stands before a noun, so what role does it play?

options.text: It is a pronoun standing alone.
It is a determiner modifying the noun.

questions.explanation: When dieser precedes a noun it functions as a determiner, not a standalone pronoun. Standing alone it would be a pronoun, but here it modifies the noun.
questions.hint: Before a noun it is a determiner.

questions.topic: A relative clause opened by a preposition
questions.learningObjective: Open a relative clause with a preposition
questions.stem: The sheet refers to a cost from last week, so how does the relative clause open?

options.text: The cost from last week, about which we spoke.
The cost from last week, which we spoke about.
The cost from last week, of which spoke we.
The cost from last week, whom we spoke about.

questions.explanation: A relative clause can be opened by a preposition plus the relative pronoun, with the preposition first. Stranding or whom are not correct for this construction.
questions.hint: Preposition plus relative pronoun opens the clause.

questions.topic: Word order in a subordinate clause with two verbs
questions.learningObjective: Order verbs in a subordinate clause
questions.stem: State the verb order in a subordinate clause with two verbs on the sheet.

answer.exemplar: In a subordinate clause with two verbs, the conjugated verb comes last after the infinitive or participle, as in the clause that the chef has ordered the truffle.

questions.explanation: German subordinate clauses send the finite verb to the end, after any infinitive or participle. This is the standard verb-final order for dependent clauses.
questions.hint: Finite verb goes to the very end.

questions.topic: A subordinate clause with a correlative conjunction

stimulus.body: The sheet links two clauses: either the truffle is fresh or the price drops.

questions.stem: Which correlative pair does the sheet use?
questions.explanation: Entweder ... oder presents two alternatives. The other pairs add, negate, or concede, so they do not fit an either-or choice on the sheet.
questions.hint: Either-or uses entweder ... oder.

questions.topic: An infinitive with zu against one without
questions.stem: On the sheet, the chef begins to cook, so does the infinitive take zu?

options.text: Yes, begin to cook always takes zu.
options.misconception: adds zu where it is not needed

options.text: No, begin to cook takes no zu.

questions.explanation: Verbs like begin, start, and try take a bare infinitive without zu. Zu appears with most other verbs in infinitive clauses.
questions.hint: Begin takes a bare infinitive.

questions.topic: An infinitive clause and its position
questions.stem: Where does the infinitive clause sit in the sentence on the sheet?

options.text: It usually follows the main clause.
It can only end the sentence.

questions.explanation: An infinitive clause with zu normally follows the main clause. Fronting is possible for emphasis but not required, and it never replaces the subject.
questions.hint: The infinitive clause follows the main clause.

questions.topic: A participle used as an adjective
questions.learningObjective: Use a participle as an adjective
questions.stem: Explain a participle used as an adjective on the sheet.

answer.exemplar: A participle used as an adjective takes adjective endings and agrees with the noun, as in the boiled egg on the costing sheet, where boiled describes the egg.

questions.explanation: Participles can become adjectives and then take normal adjective endings and agree in case, gender, and number with the noun they modify.
questions.hint: The participle takes adjective endings.

questions.topic: A participial clause and its comma

stimulus.body: The sheet writes: The truffle, sold at a premium, raises the cost. The clause sold at a premium is a participial clause.

questions.stem: How is the participial clause punctuated?

options.text: It is set off by commas.
It is followed by a semicolon.
It is set off by dashes.

questions.explanation: A non-restrictive participial clause is set off by commas. Omitting them or using other marks would mispunctuate the sentence on the sheet.
questions.hint: Commas set off the participial clause.

questions.topic: A passive sentence with a modal
questions.stem: On the sheet, the truffle must be weighed, so how is the passive formed?

options.text: The truffle is weighed by the chef.

questions.explanation: Passive with a modal uses modal plus werden plus past participle, giving must be weighed. Dropping the passive or misordering loses the meaning.
questions.hint: Modal plus werden plus participle.

questions.topic: The man form against the sich form
questions.stem: The sheet says the dish is eaten, so when is man used instead of sich?

options.text: Man is used for a general person; sich is reflexive.
Sich is used for a general person.

questions.explanation: Man expresses an unspecified agent, while sich marks a reflexive action on the subject. They are not interchangeable, and man is not restricted to plural.
questions.hint: Man is an unspecified agent.

questions.topic: A reflexive pronoun and its case
questions.stem: State the case of the reflexive pronoun when the verb takes a dative object on the sheet.

answer.exemplar: When the verb already has an accusative object, the reflexive pronoun takes the dative, as in the chef washes himself the hands, keeping the two objects distinct.

questions.explanation: A reflexive pronoun is accusative by default, but becomes dative if the verb already has an accusative object. This keeps the two objects from clashing.
questions.hint: Dative reflexive when an accusative object exists.

questions.topic: A dative object and a case-sensitive verb

stimulus.body: The sheet notes that the sauce helps the flavour. The verb help takes a dative object.

questions.stem: Which case does the object of help take?
questions.explanation: Verbs like help, follow, and believe take dative objects in German. Treating them as accusative would misstate the case on the sheet.
questions.hint: Help takes a dative object.

questions.topic: The genitive and the verbs that still require it
questions.stem: On the sheet, a verb still requires genitive, so which verb is it?
questions.explanation: Bed眉rfen still takes a genitive object, unlike help, follow, and believe, which have moved to dative. This distinction matters in formal recipe language.
questions.hint: Bed眉rfen keeps the genitive.

questions.topic: Two objects and the order they take
questions.stem: On the sheet, a dative and an accusative object appear together, so which comes first?
questions.explanation: When both objects are nouns, the dative precedes the accusative in German. Reversing them sounds unidiomatic in the recipe notes.
questions.hint: Dative comes before accusative.

questions.topic: A word order question decided by the verb
questions.learningObjective: Let the verb decide word order
questions.stem: Explain how the verb decides the order of two pronoun objects on the sheet.

answer.exemplar: When both objects are pronouns, the accusative pronoun precedes the dative pronoun, the reverse of the noun order, so the verb's object types decide the sequence.

questions.explanation: Pronoun order reverses noun order: accusative before dative. The verb type does not change this; the object form does.
questions.hint: Pronouns reverse the noun order.

questions.topic: A sentence-final verb in a question
questions.learningObjective: Place the verb in a question

stimulus.body: The sheet asks whether the truffle is fresh, using a yes-no question.

questions.stem: Where does the verb sit in that yes-no question?
questions.explanation: Yes-no questions in German put the conjugated verb first, before the subject. Verb-final order belongs to subordinate clauses, not questions.
questions.hint: Yes-no questions start with the verb.

questions.topic: An elliptical question
questions.stem: The sheet asks 'Truffle?' alone, so what kind of question is that?

options.misconception: labels a fragment as a tag

questions.explanation: An elliptical question omits parts of the sentence, leaving just a word or phrase. It is not a full yes-no or rhetorical question on the sheet.
questions.hint: A fragment question is elliptical.

questions.topic: A coordinated clause
questions.stem: On the sheet, two main clauses are joined by und, so what changes in word order?

options.text: Nothing changes; each clause keeps verb-second order.
The first clause loses its verb.
Both verbs move to the end.

questions.explanation: Coordinating conjunctions like und join main clauses without changing word order, so each keeps verb-second. Only subordinating conjunctions push the verb to the end.
questions.hint: Coordinating conjunctions keep verb-second.

questions.topic: A relative clause that refers to a possessor
questions.learningObjective: Refer to a possessor in a relative clause
questions.stem: Explain a relative clause that refers to a possessor on the sheet.

answer.exemplar: A relative clause can refer to a possessor using whose, whose form agrees with the possessor, as in the chef whose recipe is on the sheet, and it modifies the person.

questions.explanation: The possessive relative pronoun whose links to a possessor antecedent. It agrees with the possessor, not the possessed noun, in the recipe note.
questions.hint: Whose refers to the possessor.

questions.topic: A purpose clause with um ... zu

stimulus.body: The sheet says the chef weighs the truffle in order to cost the dish.

questions.stem: Which construction expresses purpose here?
questions.explanation: Um ... zu introduces an infinitive purpose clause with the same subject. Damit would require a finite clause and possibly a different subject.
questions.hint: Same subject purpose uses um ... zu.

questions.topic: A purpose clause with damit
questions.stem: On the sheet, the buyer weighs the truffle so that the chef can cost the dish, so which conjunction is used?
questions.explanation: Damit introduces a finite purpose clause, often when the subject differs. Um ... zu would not fit two different subjects on the sheet.
questions.hint: Different subjects use damit.

questions.topic: A single word that changes the claim
questions.learningObjective: Notice a word that flips the claim
questions.stem: On the sheet, adding only to the sentence changes the claim, so what does it do?

options.text: It restricts the claim to one case.

questions.explanation: A restrictive word like only narrows the claim to one case rather than negating or re-tensing it. This small word shifts the meaning on the sheet.
questions.hint: Restrictive words narrow the claim.

questions.topic: Konjunktiv I in reported speech
questions.stem: Explain how reported speech differs from direct speech on the costing sheet.

answer.exemplar: Reported speech uses Konjunktiv I and shifts pronouns and tense, while direct speech quotes the exact words, and the sheet marks reported claims with Konjunktiv forms.

questions.explanation: Reported speech signals distance and uses Konjunktiv I, whereas direct speech preserves the original wording. The sheet uses Konjunktiv forms for reported claims.
questions.hint: Reported speech uses Konjunktiv I.

questions.topic: Konjunktiv I form building

stimulus.body: The sheet reports that the cooks reduce the sauce. The verb reduce has a plural Konjunktiv I form.

questions.stem: What is the third-person plural Konjunktiv I of reduce?
questions.explanation: For many verbs the Konjunktiv I plural equals the infinitive form. Here reduzieren serves as the reported plural form on the sheet.
questions.hint: Plural Konjunktiv I often equals the infinitive.

questions.topic: Konjunktiv II for unreal conditions
questions.stem: On the sheet, if the butter were fresh, the sauce would shine, so which clause is the result?
questions.explanation: The result clause states the consequence, here the sauce would shine. The if-clause carries the unreal condition instead.
questions.hint: The result states the consequence.

questions.topic: Konjunktiv II for polite requests
questions.learningObjective: Soften a request with Konjunktiv II
questions.stem: The buyer asks politely for the truffle price, so which form softens it?

options.text: Could you tell me the price?

questions.explanation: Konjunktiv II with a modal softens the request into a polite question. A direct question or imperative lacks that distance on the sheet.
questions.hint: Modals in Konjunktiv II soften requests.

questions.topic: Konjunktiv II in a wish
questions.learningObjective: Express a wish with Konjunktiv II
questions.stem: Explain how a wish about the past uses Konjunktiv II on the sheet.

answer.exemplar: A wish about the past uses Konjunktiv II of the perfect, often with h盲tte or w盲re, as in if only the truffle had been fresh, expressing regret about a past state.

questions.explanation: Past wishes use Konjunktiv II of the perfect with h盲tte or w盲re. This expresses regret about something that did not happen, as in the recipe note.
questions.hint: Past wishes use h盲tte or w盲re.

questions.topic: A verb of feeling with the Konjunktiv II
questions.learningObjective: Combine feeling verb and Konjunktiv II

stimulus.body: The sheet records that the chef regrets the truffle was expensive.

questions.stem: Which clause carries the unreal feeling?

options.text: The clause that the truffle was expensive.

questions.explanation: The feeling verb introduces the clause, but the unreal content sits in the subordinate clause. That clause carries the Konjunktiv II on the sheet.
questions.hint: The subordinate clause carries the unreal content.

questions.topic: The w眉rde form and its limits
questions.learningObjective: Use w眉rde for verbs without simple forms
questions.stem: On the sheet, a verb lacks a simple Konjunktiv II, so what form is used?
questions.explanation: Verbs without a simple Konjunktiv II use w眉rde plus infinitive. This keeps the hypothetical meaning clear in the recipe notes.
questions.hint: No simple form means w眉rde plus infinitive.

questions.topic: Konjunktiv I without a distinct form
questions.stem: On the sheet, a verb's Konjunktiv I equals its indicative, so what happens?
questions.explanation: When Konjunktiv I is ambiguous, Konjunktiv II substitutes to signal reported speech. Keeping the indicative would blur the meaning on the sheet.
questions.hint: Konjunktiv II substitutes for ambiguity.

questions.topic: A relative clause with a preposition
questions.stem: Explain preposition placement in a relative clause on the sheet.

answer.exemplar: In a relative clause, the preposition precedes the relative pronoun, as in the pan with which the chef cooks, keeping the preposition attached to the pronoun.

questions.explanation: German relative clauses keep the preposition before the relative pronoun. Stranding it after the verb is not standard in the recipe notes.
questions.hint: Preposition before the relative pronoun.

questions.topic: A relative pronoun in the dative

stimulus.body: The sheet refers to the sauce to which salt is added. The relative pronoun is in the dative.

questions.stem: Which form is the dative relative pronoun for a feminine noun?
questions.explanation: For a feminine singular antecedent in the dative, the relative pronoun is der. Dem is masculine or neuter, den is plural, and die is nominative.
questions.hint: Feminine dative relative pronoun is der.

questions.topic: A demonstrative pronoun in a subordinate clause
questions.stem: On the sheet, a demonstrative pronoun opens a reported clause, so which is it?
questions.explanation: The demonstrative pronoun der can open a subordinate clause referring back to a statement. The other forms do not serve this pronominal role on the sheet.
questions.hint: Der works as a demonstrative pronoun.

questions.topic: A demonstrative determiner used as a pronoun
questions.stem: On the sheet, dieser stands alone, so what role does it play?

options.text: It is a pronoun standing alone.
It is a determiner modifying a noun.

questions.explanation: When dieser stands alone without a noun, it functions as a demonstrative pronoun. Before a noun it would be a determiner, as on the sheet.
questions.hint: Standing alone it is a pronoun.

questions.topic: A relative clause opened by a preposition
questions.stem: Explain opening a relative clause with a preposition on the sheet.

answer.exemplar: A relative clause can be opened by a preposition followed by the relative pronoun, as in the cost about which we spoke, keeping the preposition at the front.

questions.explanation: The preposition precedes the relative pronoun to open the clause. This keeps the construction compact and standard in the recipe notes.
questions.hint: Preposition plus relative pronoun opens it.

questions.topic: Word order in a subordinate clause with two verbs
questions.learningObjective: Order two verbs in subordinate clause

stimulus.body: The sheet contains a clause: that the chef has ordered the truffle.

questions.stem: Where does the finite verb sit?

options.text: At the end, after the participle.

questions.explanation: In a subordinate clause the finite verb goes last, after the participle or infinitive. Placing it earlier would break the verb-final order on the sheet.
questions.hint: Finite verb comes last.

questions.topic: A subordinate clause with a correlative conjunction
questions.stem: On the sheet, neither the truffle nor the butter is fresh, so which pair is used?
questions.explanation: Weder ... noch expresses negative coordination. The other pairs present alternatives, additions, or concessions, so they do not fit the sheet.
questions.hint: Negative pairs use weder ... noch.

questions.topic: An infinitive with zu against one without
questions.stem: On the sheet, the chef can cook, so does the infinitive take zu?

options.text: No, modal verbs take a bare infinitive.

questions.explanation: Modal verbs like can take a bare infinitive without zu. Adding zu would be wrong in the recipe note.
questions.hint: Modals take bare infinitives.

questions.topic: An infinitive clause and its position
questions.stem: Explain the position of an infinitive clause on the sheet.

answer.exemplar: An infinitive clause with zu normally follows the main clause, as in the chef plans to weigh the truffle, and it can be fronted for emphasis without changing the core meaning.

questions.explanation: The default position is after the main clause. Fronting is possible for emphasis but not required in the recipe notes.
questions.hint: It follows the main clause by default.

questions.topic: A participle used as an adjective

stimulus.body: The sheet describes a boiled egg in the recipe.

questions.stem: How does the participle function?

options.text: As a verb in past tense.
options.misconception: treats it as a finite verb

questions.explanation: The participle boiled functions as an adjective modifying egg and takes adjective endings. It is not a finite verb, adverb, or noun on the sheet.
questions.hint: The participle modifies the noun.

questions.topic: A participial clause and its comma
questions.stem: On the sheet, a participial clause is non-restrictive, so how is it punctuated?
questions.explanation: A non-restrictive participial clause is set off by commas on both sides. Other marks or none would mispunctuate the sentence on the sheet.
questions.hint: Commas set it off.

questions.topic: A passive sentence with a modal
questions.stem: On the sheet, the truffle can be weighed, so which form is correct?
questions.explanation: Passive with a modal uses modal plus werden plus participle, giving can be weighed. Dropping the passive or misordering loses the meaning on the sheet.
questions.hint: Modal plus werden plus participle.

questions.topic: The man form against the sich form
questions.stem: Explain the difference between man and sich on the sheet.

answer.exemplar: Man expresses an unspecified agent, as in man eats the dish, while sich marks a reflexive action on the subject, and the sheet keeps these two constructions separate.

questions.explanation: Man is an impersonal agent, whereas sich is reflexive. Confusing them would misstate who acts in the recipe note.
questions.hint: Man is impersonal; sich is reflexive.

questions.topic: A reflexive pronoun and its case

stimulus.body: The sheet says the chef washes his hands. The reflexive pronoun takes dative here.

questions.stem: Why is the reflexive pronoun dative?

options.text: Because the verb takes an accusative object already.
Because the verb is reflexive by default.

questions.explanation: When the verb already has an accusative object, the reflexive pronoun becomes dative. Number or tense do not decide the case on the sheet.
questions.hint: Dative reflexive when an accusative object exists.

questions.topic: A dative object and a case-sensitive verb
questions.stem: On the sheet, the sauce helps the flavour, so which case is the object?
questions.explanation: Help takes a dative object in German. Treating it as accusative, genitive, or nominative would misstate the case on the sheet.
questions.hint: Help takes dative.

questions.topic: The genitive and the verbs that still require it
questions.stem: On the sheet, a verb still requires genitive, so which is it?
questions.explanation: Bed眉rfen still takes genitive, unlike help, follow, and believe. This distinction remains in formal recipe language on the sheet.
questions.hint: Bed眉rfen keeps genitive.

questions.topic: Two objects and the order they take
questions.stem: Explain the order of two noun objects on the sheet.

answer.exemplar: When both objects are nouns, the dative precedes the accusative, so the sheet lists the recipient before the thing given in the sentence.

questions.explanation: Dative before accusative is the default for two noun objects. Reversing them sounds unidiomatic in the recipe notes.
questions.hint: Dative before accusative for nouns.

questions.topic: A word order question decided by the verb

stimulus.body: The sheet contains a sentence with two pronoun objects.

questions.stem: Which pronoun comes first?
questions.explanation: When both objects are pronouns, the accusative precedes the dative, reversing noun order. This rule applies in the recipe note on the sheet.
questions.hint: Pronouns reverse: accusative first.

questions.topic: A sentence-final verb in a question
questions.stem: On the sheet, a yes-no question is asked, so where does the verb sit?
questions.explanation: Yes-no questions in German put the conjugated verb first. Verb-final order belongs to subordinate clauses, not questions on the sheet.
questions.hint: Yes-no questions start with the verb.
